items.title: Copyright, Edition and Citations
items.core: Describe the version, title, author signature, license, non-medical advice, source rules and citation methods of "The Advanced Guide to Life", and indicate that this book does not have a publishing organization and ISBN.
body: Version and book title: The current version is 1.1.0, updated on 2026-11-23. The Chinese title is "Advanced Guide to Life: An Ordinary Person's Failure, Recovery and Relearning"; the English title is Still Here: A Field Guide to Beginning Again. Directory names part-1, part-2, etc. are historical subject identifiers, not reading order. The reading order of the books is based on the road map of the book and the table of contents on each page. When the version number changes, the published Chinese and English EPUB and PDF will be rebuilt at the same time; the file check value is published in the download center, and the build list is saved in the download directory.

Author and English version description: Author: Han Xiankai. The English version is signed Han Xiankai. The Chinese version is the main version. The English version is an independently rewritten version, not a word-for-word translation: the chapter structure and dates correspond to the evidence, but the tone, examples, and sentence length are rewritten to suit the reading habits of English readers. If there are differences in understanding between the two languages, the facts and boundaries of the Chinese version shall prevail, and the differences will be reported to the maintainer. "Outrageous" is the pen name used by the author in his early days and is also the source of the 2017 "Outrageous English Learning Guide". It is retained on this page and in the prologue as a historical note, and is no longer used as a title or regular byline; the English version does not transliterate this pseudonym.

License: Text, translations, graphics and templates created by the author: CC BY-NC 4.0. It can be copied, adapted and distributed non-commercially, and it must be signed by byoungd and contributors, linked to this repository, and the source page and modifications are indicated. Commercial use is not covered by this license. Site configuration, check scripts, building code and testing: MIT. Third-party references, images, trademarks and product names: remain the property of their respective rights holders and will not be relicensed for inclusion in this repository. This repository is an open content project, not open source software in the OSI sense; only the code part is open source software licensed under MIT. For complete instructions, see LICENSE.md, LICENSE-CONTENT.md, and LICENSE-CODE.md in the root directory of the repository.

Not medical advice: The content in the book about depression, anxiety, recovery, sleep and workload is a compilation of personal experience and public information and does not constitute diagnosis, treatment plan, medication advice or crisis intervention. The recovery chapter does not provide drug names, dosages, or discontinuation protocols, nor does it provide local hotline numbers that may have expired. If you are experiencing persistent depression, insomnia, hopelessness, or thoughts of harming yourself, start by contacting someone you trust and seek support from a qualified medical or psychological professional in your area. Ensure safety first, then talk about growth. This book is not a substitute for care.

Citation and review: Statements in the book are divided into three categories: research conclusions, personal experience, and hypotheses to be tested. Only the first type can be directly retold as evidence; the second type only proves that the author has experienced it; and the third type must be retested by the reader on his or her own task. AI products, model capabilities, prices, protocols and supplier policies are reviewed in stages according to the speed of change: 30 days for usage policies, security bulletins, product functions and packages; 60 days for protocol specifications and implementation guidelines; and 120 days for stable concepts. The sources_checked date on the page indicates that the external data was verified, and the updated date indicates that the text was modified. The two cannot replace each other. See the Materials, Citations and Verification Instructions for complete source rules, and the References for a list of entries.

Correction and feedback: factual errors, broken links, translation differences: submit through the question template, clearly stating the page, original text, source and suggestions. Security issues, compromised personal information, or unauthorized third-party images: Do not post publicly, report via SECURITY.md's private channels. Reader practice receipts: Reader practice receipts may be used, but please remove unnecessary third-party identity, health, financial and relationship details. Revisions will be included in the text and EPUB/PDF when next released; historical versions can be viewed through Git commit records.

No publishing organization and ISBN: This book is an open manuscript maintained by the author. It is not published by a publishing house, has no ISBN assigned, and has no paper book distribution channels. EPUB and PDF are generated by the build script of this repository and are suitable for personal reading and home printing. They do not represent review or endorsement by any publishing organization. When citing this book, please use the title, author, version number, update date and website, and indicate that the text adopts CC BY-NC 4.0. The repository provides CITATION.cff for direct reference in tools that support this format:

If an official published version appears in the future, this page will add the corresponding relationship between the publisher, ISBN and version; before then, please do not fill in any ISBN or publishing institution for this book.

items.title: Prologue: Don’t rush to change your life yet
items.core: Start from a real fall: after the company went bankrupt, the body lost control, and the relationship was damaged, how did an ordinary person catch himself, then relearn English, use AI, create works, and let the changes stand the test of time.
body: That question from 2017: In July 2017, my friend W. was preparing for the TOEFL. She asked me: "How can I learn English effectively?" At that time, I thought it was just a question about vocabulary, grammar and learning methods. So I wrote down the detours I took: how to memorize words, how to practice listening, how to make an original book no longer look like a wall, and how to speak the first imperfect sentence of English when I dare not speak. Later I discovered that what she was really asking was maybe another thing: How can an ordinary person move forward a little bit in the face of limited time, repeated setbacks, and an unideal life? It took me many years to understand this question. English is a concrete door: you can use it to read an article without translation, understand a work meeting, write a letter to someone far away, and get an extra perspective when the information is confusing. But after the door is opened, what you have to face is still yourself - how to arrange time, how to treat your body, how to endure failure, how to turn an idea into a work, how to continue to take care of the people in front of you after losing something. I once imagined life as a constantly upgrading game route: if you complete a goal, you will get the next piece of equipment; if you make enough money, you will have stable happiness; if you make a product, you will prove that your past choices were not wrong. Later, when my company collapsed, my body lost control, and my relationships and self-esteem hit rock bottom, I realized that life is more like a room that needs to be rearranged every day. The dust left yesterday is still there today; a piece of broken furniture cannot be repaired by louder slogans; the weather outside the window never listens to our arrangements. The so-called advancement often means just cleaning the floor, saying what should be apologized, sending the body to the doctor, and completing the step that can be completed today.

What this book will give you: So, this is not a book that promises you to "become great". It only wants to provide four things, in the order I need them: A set of ways to catch myself first: safety, sleep, help, restoring shame to facts, and allowing myself to complete only the smallest step when the capacity is very small; An executable English learning path: let input, output, feedback and review form a cycle, making English the first training ground for re-entering the world; A set with AI Collaborative learning method: let tools help you develop judgment, instead of avoiding thinking for you, and not outsourcing source, privacy and responsibility; a ninety-day action plan and a set of real records: giving the content read a chance to become works, feedback and a new rhythm of life, and also allowing personal experience to be tested by evidence.

How to read this book: You don't have to read from the first page to the last. If you are at a trough, read my story and the recovery chapter first. Your goal today can be just to get through the day safely. If you have stabilized and want to start learning again, start from Part 2: Relearning and open the input. If you have a lot of information but no works, read the Use AI to Learn Everything and the Ninety Days Action chapter first. The complete reading route, the entrance by question and the traces that can be left in each chapter are all placed in the reading map of how to read the book and the appendix. This page is only responsible for getting you through the door. Please treat each chapter as a workbench rather than an exam. Take away only one thing after reading: a sentence, an exercise, a habit you need to stop, or an idea to start again. If knowledge does not leave traces in life, it is just a beautiful road sign.

Written to the person who is opening this book at this moment: Maybe you are sitting on the subway commuting, and the screen of your mobile phone is full of collections; maybe you have just ended a relationship and are wondering whether you can only stop here from now on; maybe you are pushed into the corner by work, debt, exams or illness, and even the word "effort" sounds tired. I am not qualified to guarantee that tomorrow will get better for you. All I can say is this: People's lives are usually not saved by one huge victory, but slowly held up by many small, repetitive, and unapplauded actions. Remember five words today, listen to real English for ten minutes tomorrow, write a piece of text that is not beautiful the day after tomorrow; finish a small thing that has been put off for a long time, send a message to someone who should apologize, eat on time, and turn off the lights early. They may seem unrelated, but together they constitute new evidence that I still have some influence over my life. This impact does not have to be grand, but it must be real. May you start here not to become someone else, but to become more completely yourself.

items.title: How to read this book
items.core: Give readers who open "Advanced Guide to Life" for the first time an alternative route: read the story first or learn the method first, how to enter according to the questions, how to come back after the interruption, and the promises that this page can leave.
body: Two reading methods, used in turn: a complete reading arc. Complete reading from beginning to postscript, going through four changes: · Stages · Reading scope · What is left after reading · · Catching yourself · Prologue · My story · Recovery · One page of real situations that can be reviewed: facts, costs, boundaries and next steps · · Re-learning · Part 2: Re-learning, open the input and its chapters · An English proficiency baseline, an evidence card and a startable training cycle · · Amplification and delivery · Part 3: Borrowing tools to amplify abilities · Part 4: Practice and recovery · An authentic delivery, a source record and a retestable work · · Hand over time · Part 5: Action and long-term change · Part 6: Become a lifelong friend with yourself · Postscript · A ninety-day plan, a cycle review and a more stable self-relationship · Read like a studio Jump straight to the point in front of you from reading a map, table of contents, or index of terms and methods. Pause after reading a section, write down a sentence of judgment, do an exercise, or save a first version sample; after a while, use the evidence chain template and weekly review template to check whether it has been transferred to new tasks. You don't need to memorize the entire book, just make your next move clearer. There is no conflict between these two readings. Read the complete guide to help you understand why the method is arranged the way it is, and read on-demand to help you put the method to work today.

Each chapter leaves four traces: after reading a chapter, don’t just mark it as “read”. Please leave at least two of the following four: · A trace · A question to answer · An example · · A judgment · What am I more sure of now than before I read it? · “Only tracking one main issue this week.” · · A sample · What output proves I did it? · A recording, an email, a list of mistakes · · A boundary · What things cannot be left to tools or imagination? · Do not upload customer privacy; do not write a single experience into a pattern · · One return visit point · When and under what conditions should a retest be conducted? · Change the topic and redo the same task after seven days · If after reading a chapter, you only think "makes sense", don't continue to collect it. Reword it into an action that can be seen by others and reviewed by yourself.

When plans are interrupted, come back here: interruptions are not an exception to the approach, but a reality that it must be able to withstand. Open the learning status first and mark what has been completed, what has not yet been confirmed, the costs incurred, and the next step; if the capacity changes, go back to the minimum feasible day or rhythm ledger, and don’t re-weight the plan with shame. Wait until a repeatable rhythm returns before adding tasks back. A truly reliable system is never continuous, but still knows how to get home after an interruption.

A one-page promise to the reader: Before moving on to the next page, you can write four sentences: The real problem I want to deal with now is: The baseline evidence I already have is: After this reading, when will I complete which minimal action: What information, privacy, health or relationship boundaries must be kept by myself: These four sentences are enough to start. Reading is not about leaving life, reading is about regaining the direction in which life can be seen. To choose an entrance based on specific questions, prepare for overseas job interviews, help a junior high school learner, or check whether you have made real changes, you can go to Reading Map to view the complete table.

items.title: Who is this book suitable for and who is not suitable for it?
items.core: An honest explanation of who the "Advanced Guide to Life" is for and who it is not for, as well as two letters to young people and people who are at a trough, to help readers decide whether to continue.
body: Who it’s suitable for: People who want to learn something by themselves. You don’t need to sign up for a class, wait for a teacher, or gather tools. All you need is a real task, a baseline, and a date when you’re willing to retest. Someone who is returning from a hiatus. Job losses, failed startups, physical problems, relationship endings, extended periods of stagnation—the book has a path from recovery to relearning, not just a “buck it up.” People who use AI at work but don’t want to hand over judgment. You'll see how to build provenance, privacy, acceptance, and responsibility into tasks instead of letting the tool decide for you. A parent or teacher who is studying with a child. The family learning chapter separates time, accounts, data boundaries and "who makes decisions" to avoid putting adults' anxieties on children. Readers who are willing to accept that "there is no unified answer." The book distinguishes between research conclusions, personal experience, and hypotheses to be tested; it wants you to retest rather than copy.

Who it may not be suitable for: People who only want to improve scores, memorize templates, and answer questions in the short term. There is no list of exam tips, and no scores are promised. People who are looking for the formula for success or the shortcut to wealth. The author writes about failure, cost, and recovery, not "how to turn around quickly." A person who is in acute crisis and requires immediate professional care. If you are experiencing thoughts of harming yourself or experiencing severe physical symptoms at the moment, please contact emergency services, a trusted person or local qualified professional support before returning to school. This book is not a substitute for care. People who want a complete English course. The English part is a training protocol and evidence card, not a systematic teaching material from phonetic notation to writing; it assumes that you are willing to find materials, do tasks, and accept feedback on your own. People who want books to make decisions for you. The book provides a framework and boundaries for judgment, but does not give an answer to "what your life should be like."

Written to young people: You don’t have to be in your twenties to find a direction that is always right. Many directions do not appear after thinking clearly, but slowly emerge from the fog after doing several small projects, seeing several kinds of work, and bearing the results several times. More reliable than picking the perfect track is retaining the ability to learn, deliver and turn. If career anxiety keeps you collecting courses, certificates, and success stories, you might as well switch to a small project that can be completed in two weeks: solve a problem of someone around you, make a working tool, write an article with a source, or improve a process for real users. A project can fail, but it will tell you what you like, what's missing, whether it can be delivered, and whether others will want to use it again.

For those who are going through a slump: Losing your job, failing a business, ending a relationship, damaging your health, and being confused for long periods of time can all really sap your energy. Lows are not a test that must be won immediately. What you can do today may be to get a relatively complete night's sleep, eat a meal, go outdoors, or say "I need help now" to a trusted person. These things make sense on their own, without having to package them into a growth report first. Pausing is not giving up, asking for help is not weakness, and recalibrating is not backsliding. Wait until your strength comes back before deciding whether to increase the weight. The personal stories here are not medical or psychotherapeutic advice; if depression, insomnia, hopelessness, or dangerous thoughts persist, please contact trusted relatives and friends and seek local qualified medical or psychological professional support. Ensure safety first, then talk about growth.

Continue reading: If you have decided to continue, How to Read this book will give you three reading paths and four traces you can leave. If your capacity is very small at the moment, read Recovery: Catch Yourself First, or see from my story how another person started from the bottom. If you just want to do one small thing first, open the learning status template and write down the questions, clues, minimal actions, and boundaries.

items.title: Roadmap of this book
items.core: Using a six-part structure table and three reading paths to explain the reading order of "Advanced Guide to Life", what is left at each step, and how to start when the capacity is small.
body: Structure of the book: · Part · What does this part ask · Entrance · · Prologue and opening · Why am I willing to start over? What does this book have in store for me? · Prologue · How to read this book · · Part 1: Put yourself back into life · When failure, body, relationship and career are out of order, how to catch yourself first? · Introduction to this part · My story · · Part 2: Relearning, opening up input · After recovery, how to retrain attention and ability with a specific thing? · Introduction to this part · CEFR self-assessment · · Part 3: Using tools to amplify capabilities · How to use AI without handing over judgment, privacy and responsibility? · Introduction to this part · Use AI to learn everything · · Part 4: Practice and recovery · How to bring learning back to the body, family and daily life, and come back after interruption? · Introduction to this part · First week of practice · · Part 5: Action and long-term change · How to turn a round of practice into a real work and let it still have echoes ninety days later? · Introduction to this part · Ninety Days of Action · · Part 6: Be a lifelong friend with yourself · How to understand, treat yourself well, improve yourself, and get along with yourself for a long time? · Understand yourself · Postscript · Table of contents names part-2, part-1, etc. are historical theme identifiers, not reading order. The order of the books is based on this table and the table of contents: first (Story and Recovery), then Part 2 (Relearning).

Three reading paths: Story first, suitable for people who want to be understood more than learning methods first. Prologue → My Story; I'm Still Here → Recovery Chapter; Choice Chapter → Relationship Chapter; Enter the second introduction when you have enough energy. Method first is suitable for people who come with a specific task and want to start as soon as possible. CEFR self-test → Principles of cognition and training; Choose a main line among vocabulary, grammar, listening, reading, speaking, and writing, and complete a fourteen-day experiment; Use AI to learn everything → Works; First week of practice → Ninety-day action. When the capacity is small, it is suitable for people whose physical or emotional state does not allow reading for a long time. Read only the "Load Reduction" section in the recovery chapter and do not do the exercises; Open the learning status template and write only four lines: question, clue, minimum action, boundary; That's it for today. Put the rhythm ledger to tomorrow or next week, and don’t make up any homework. The three paths can be swapped midway. When you read the story and you want to do something, you turn to the method; when you are unable to do the method, you return to recovery. The structure of the book allows for round tripping.

There are only five minutes today: If you only have a small gap now, don’t try to start a book: Open the study status template; Write down the most real problem in front of you; Write down the smallest action that can be completed today; Write down a boundary that must be maintained (privacy, body, relationship or money). These four lines are a beginning. Five minutes doesn’t need to produce a conclusion, just take the next step out of the fog.

After reading: After the main text, there are appendices, arranged by purpose: first check the terminology and method index, and then enter the reading map by question; when you need to do something, open the toolbox overview; when you want to cite or check sources, look at the references and materials, citation and verification instructions; if you want to understand how this book was produced, you can read the book case in the appendix. If you finish reading, the most valuable thing to leave behind is not "I finished reading", but a real delivery, a record of retesting, or a decision that you are willing to check back in ninety days. Put them into the ninety-day action list.

items.title: Part 2: Re-learn and open input
items.core: After catching yourself, start again from the specific training ground of English: establish a real baseline, let the input go through recall, expression and feedback, and become an ability that can be used in new scenarios.
body: The question this section wants to answer: What can I accomplish in listening, speaking, reading, and writing now, rather than "roughly what level is the overall level"? How does a word, a sound, or an article go from being seen before to being used in new situations? How does input become an ability independent of raw materials through recall, expression and feedback? Why do structures still change time, responsibility, conditions, or certainty in real expressions when the rules have already been seen? At what point can AI help with practice, and at what point does it have to quit and let me complete it on my own? When English enters job hunting, interviews and remote collaboration, how to rewrite the level direction into job tasks and evidence? Don't use the weakest one to deny all abilities, and don't use the strongest one to cover up the real gaps. The starting point is not a verdict, but a map that gives direction to the next step.

Reading path: · Path · Chapter · Things to stay · · Confirm the starting point · CEFR goals and self-assessment of English proficiency · An unmodified baseline for each of listening, speaking, reading and writing · Establishment method · Cognition and training principles · Vocabulary system · Grammar · A real scene, a set of reusable word chunks, a high-impact structure and retest date · · Open comprehension · Listening training · Reading training · Main point reconstruction, difficulty classification and source recording · · Entering expression · Oral training · Writing training · First version, feedback, revised version and expression under new conditions · · Using tools · Learning English with AI · AI intervention boundary, independent retest and real audience feedback · · Entering the job · Job-seeking English · Job language map, unfamiliar questioning, asynchronous writing and fourteen days of evidence · No need to advance all chapters at the same time. Start by choosing a task that will happen in real life: a meeting, an email, a document, a note, or a conversation. Open the required abilities around it and keep the rest of the chapter quiet for now.

What to leave behind after reading: At the end of this part, please leave at least three things: A starting point sample that can be redone thirty days later, including unmodified structural choices; An English output that a real audience can understand, respond to, or use; if the goal is to apply for a job, include at least one stranger questioning or asynchronous handover; An evidence chain that states the time, conditions, and next variable. If all that’s left is the collection, the playtime, and the feeling of “learning a lot”, you haven’t finished this one yet. Turn off the material, change to a similar task, and do it again independently. Ability is the part that remains after the prompt has left.

Enter the text: Let’s not ask ourselves whether we are “good at English”. Start by taking out a piece of paper and save the version you can finish today. Doors don’t open until you’re fully prepared. Many times, it is you who reaches out and pushes first, and then the light comes in through the gap.

items.title: CEFR Objectives and English Proficiency Self-Assessment
items.core: Use the "what can be done" description of A1-C2 to diagnose the starting point of listening, speaking, reading and writing, and convert the level into checkable 7-day, 30-day and 12-week tasks.
body: Quick overview of this chapter: Save unmodified baselines for listening, speaking, reading, and writing; Translate A1–C2 directions into specific scenarios, tasks, quality thresholds, and deadlines; Arrange practice in 7-day, 30-day, and 12-week cadences instead of chasing an average grade; Retest with the same conditions, parallel tasks, and external feedback to determine the next variable.

A1-C2: What I can do: · Level · Observable overall performance · · A1 · Can understand and use very common expressions; interact simply when the other person speaks slowly and is willing to help. · · A2 · Able to handle direct communication on familiar topics such as personal information, shopping, places, work, etc. · · B1 · Able to understand the main meaning of familiar topics; cope with it in travel and daily situations, and briefly explain experiences, plans and reasons. · · B2 · Able to understand the main points of concrete or abstract complex texts; interact more naturally with skilled users and express positions clearly. · · C1 · Able to understand demanding, lengthy material and grasp its underlying meaning; express flexibly in academic, professional and social settings. · · C2 · Can understand what he hears or reads with almost complete ease; can synthesize sources, reconstruct arguments, and express nuances with precision. · Source: Council of Europe, CEFR 3.3 Global Scale, accessed 2026-08-16. The above table is a Chinese summary for ease of use and is not an official translation.

Quick Evidence of Four Competencies: Pick a topic that is relevant to your real life and complete the following tasks. Don’t look up words to complete the first version, save the original sample. · Competencies · 10–20 minute tasks · Checkpoints · · Listening · Listen to 2–4 minutes of material, write down the main idea, 3 details, and repeat it · Main idea, details, chunk boundaries, reasons for omission · · Reading · Read an article of 600–1000 words, write a five-sentence summary and a question · Main ideas, evidence, inferences, and whether new words hinder understanding · · Speaking · 2 minutes without reading the transcript, explaining experiences, ideas, or processes · Comprehensibility, pauses, grammar, chunks, task completion · · Writing · 20 minutes to write a 180–250 word email, note, or essay · Purpose, structure, argumentation, accuracy, ability to revise · Write sample and self-evaluation into English Proficiency Diagnosis. If the four items are very different, grade them separately and do not force an average.

Don’t let the four average scores obscure collaboration skills: listening, reading, speaking, and writing are necessary entrances, but real learning and work often require you to hand over information to others, advance things in asynchronous conversations, and repair misunderstandings in a timely manner when they arise. These are task dimensions and are not intended to be an additional level beyond A1–C2; the evidence can be kept separately within the same diagnostic form. · Task dimensions · 10–15 minute sample · Through evidence · · Paraphrasing and mediation · Read two short pieces of material with different positions, explaining their respective claims, differences and what is still unknown in English · The audience can distinguish the two views, your paraphrase and your inference, without polishing the conflict into consistency · · Online interaction · In a real or simulated asynchronous thread, write a progress, a blockage and the next step · The other party knows who is responsible, when to continue, and what information is missing without a meeting · · Misunderstandings are fixed · Ask for clarification in the conversation, and then restate the consensus and open issues in your own words · The other party confirms that your retelling is accurate and the next step is not changed by guessing · If one of the tasks, courses, or family collaborations rarely involves it, you can ignore it for the time being; if it is a high-risk link in reality, do not replace it with speaking or writing scores. When you need more specific job samples, go to the English for Job Search section and put these dimensions back into the actual job description and evidence card.

From level to goal: An effective goal should include: scenarios, tasks, quality thresholds, deadlines, and evidence. After 12 weeks, I can explain the background, progress, and risks in a 5-minute work report; the audience can repeat the key points without switching to Chinese; I save the recordings and feedback forms for weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12. "From B1 to B2" can be used as a direction, but cannot be used as a training goal alone. Progression is usually not uniform and cannot be guaranteed by the number of hours of study. If the real goal is overseas positions or remote interviews, do not write B1, B2 or C1 as the unified recruitment line. Enter the job hunting English section first, use a real job to test project descriptions, unfamiliar questions, interactive repairs and asynchronous writing, and then let the sub-item performance determine the next variable.

7-Day Startup: Day 1: Complete four baselines, saving one unmodified sample each. Days 2–5: Choose one item each day and do “Input → Active Recall → Output → Feedback” for 25–45 minutes. Day 6: Repeat the weakest task and compare whether similar errors are reduced. Day 7: Fill in the weekly review and determine only one key point for next week.

30 days to establish a system: complete at least one checkable task each week in listening, speaking, reading and writing; the frequency of key abilities can be increased. Establish error categories: comprehension, vocabulary/chunks, pronunciation, grammar, structure, strategy, attention. Rework old tasks or parallel tasks of the same difficulty once a week and compare performance rather than feelings. Retest on the 30th day using the same topic and duration, retaining before and after samples and external feedback.

12 weeks to complete the migration: Weeks 1–4: Establish a steady rhythm with tasks just below the frustration threshold. Weeks 5–8: Increase material complexity and time pressure to practice transfer across topics. Weeks 9–11: Simulate real exam, conference, presentation, reading or writing delivery. Week 12: Complete final tasks, blind review or ask real readers/listeners for feedback to determine the next cycle.

Feedback scale: 0–2 points for each item: 0=not completed, 1=partially completed, 2=stable completion. Task Accomplished: Are the message and intent conveyed? Comprehensibility: Can the other person understand you without guessing? Accuracy and scope: Do the vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, or spelling support the task? Organization and flow: Is the message coherent, and do pauses disrupt communication? Revision and migration: Can improvements be made after receiving feedback and reused in new tasks? The total score is only used for longitudinal comparison of the same person and is not used to label others. If you continue to lose points in "accuracy and range", don't lump all the problems into "poor grammar." First confirm whether the error changes time, participants, negation, conditional or certainty, and then use the grammar chapter and grammar evidence card to track a structure that affects the task; low-impact deviations can be postcoded.

Bring self-assessment into the next cycle: This scale only describes your performance in a task and does not declare for you that you have "reached a certain level." After completing the self-test, please bring the results into the evidence section: How to make changes visible: Save today's baseline and do not overwrite it with a revised version; Record your immediate performance after practice and write down what help you received; Remove the most recent reminder after seven days and complete a delayed-and-hold retest; Change the topic, audience, or task after thirty or ninety days to check whether migration has occurred. If the four abilities are very different, trace their evidence chains separately. The value of self-assessment is not to give yourself a beautiful label, but to give yourself a comparable starting point for the next exercise. Use the Chain of Evidence template when you need to put four time points on the same page, don't just keep the final score.

Conclusion: Levels are just coordinates: a level can tell you how far a certain task is, but it cannot tell you why you want to go, nor can it walk for you. A2, B1 or C1 are just descriptions of performance under certain conditions, not a person’s upper limit, nor a qualification to be liked, trusted or seen. Real changes are often quieter than grades: the first time you understand a stranger's request, the first time you finish your reasons in a meeting, the first time you write an email that doesn't require the other party to second-guess. They may not cause the label to change immediately, but they have given you another passable road between you and the world. So save today's score, and save today's clumsiness. The next time I come back, it's not to prove that I'm worthy of a certain letter, but to see what I can do more completely. The meaning of coordinates is to help people find the way, not to pin them in place.

items.title: Cognition: Turn effort into verifiable learning
items.core: Use real tasks, first version baseline, active recall, feedback, intervals, recovery and cross-session status to turn effort into comparable and transferable evidence of learning.
body: Quick overview of this chapter: Rewrite "I want to make progress" into audience, actions, quality thresholds, deadlines and evidence; Distinguish between research conclusions, personal experience and hypotheses waiting to be tested; Save an unpolished first version to avoid the finished product covering the starting point; Use input, active recall, output, feedback and recording to form a complete learning loop; Classify errors by task impact and do not attribute all failures to laziness or vocabulary; Let feedback change the next action instead of just adding notes and suggestions; Schedule intervals based on performance to protect sleep, body, and minimum capacity for regression; Write goals, examples, errors, and next steps into learning states outside of sessions; Test transfer under new topics, audiences, modalities, or time pressures.

1. First define a real delivery: "Learn English", "Learn programming" and "Improve expression" are all too big to decide what to do today. Start by writing clearly: · Elements · Problem · Example · · Audience · Who will understand, decide, or act based on this? · New colleagues, clients, teachers, yourself · · Actions · What will the other party do after reading, listening or watching? · Repeat, Reply, Run, Select, Continue · · Input · Which specific material are you working on? · 2 minutes of audio, API documentation, an email · · Quality thresholds · What counts as done, and what risks are unacceptable? · State the purpose and responsibilities; don’t miss limits · · Conditions · What are the time limits, equipment, context, allowed tools? · 20 minutes, no subtitles, searchable · · Evidence · Which work, test or real response survives? · Recording, retelling, running results, email reply · The target sentence can be written like this: Within 12 weeks, I can explain the background, progress and risks in a 5-minute work report; the audience can retell the key points without switching languages; I save the recordings and feedback from weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12. It’s a better guide to action than “from B1 to B2.” Grades may describe performance under certain conditions but are not a substitute for scenarios, tasks, deadlines, and evidence.

2. Separate three categories of words: This guide will put different evidence in different places: Research support: the results observed under specific samples, conditions and measurements; it tells you what is worth trying, and does not guarantee that everyone will get the same results; Personal experience: explains why I made a certain choice; it has narrative value and is also a clue for designing experiments, but it is not a universal rule; Hypothesis to be tested: a judgment that there is currently insufficient evidence; write it as the next action, counterexample or pause condition. When a piece of advice does not describe the object, conditions, outcome indicators, and sources, put it back in the hypothesis area. Just because a method makes sense doesn't mean it's right for your task.

3. A complete learning loop: 25-45 minutes each time, try to go through the following six steps: Definition: Write down the task, audience, conditions and completion standards; First version: Complete it once independently with the minimum help allowed and save the original sample; Diagnosis: Locate the failure to language, structure, background, strategy, attention, capacity or equipment; Directed input: Only fill in the information required for the current error and avoid continuing without boundaries; Active output: close the material, retell, write, speak, run or make decisions; Feedback and status: record the results, help, still unknown and a condition to be changed next time. "Finishing it" is not the seventh step. The end point of the learning loop is: after the tools and materials are gone, you can still complete a similar action, or know more accurately why you can't complete it.
4. The first edition is a measurement, not a judgment: the first edition does not have to be beautiful, but it must be comparable. Note:

Do not overwrite the first version with a later polished version, and do not write the first failure as stable ability. The first edition only answers one question: What could I have done independently under these conditions? If there are four English abilities, use the English proficiency diagnosis to record listening, reading, speaking, and writing; if the bottleneck in a certain item is more specific, enter the corresponding evidence card.

5. Diagnose errors instead of judging yourself: A poor performance may come from different levels: · Level · Typical performance · Next question · · Language form · Word form, sound, grammar or spelling not recognized · Which form changes the meaning? · · Structure and meaning · Know the word, but do not understand the subject, time, condition or relationship · Which relationship cannot be explained? · · Background and concepts · I can read the language, but I don’t know the object and premise · Which domain knowledge is missing? · · Strategies and Tools · Check the same place repeatedly, or the prompt cannot be removed · Which stent should be retained and when should it be removed? · · Attention and capacity · Errors are concentrated in the second half, and the body declines significantly · What is the minimum sustainable task today? · · Environment and equipment · Sound, network, fonts, and interface affect the results · Does the performance change after changing the device? · “Careless”, “untalented” and “insufficient vocabulary” are often labels that end the diagnosis prematurely. Save the error samples first and then choose only the one variable that most affects the task. The purpose of diagnosis is not to find a personality explanation for the failure, but to find a changeable condition for the next practice.

6. Active recall is more stringent than familiarity: Repeated exposure can make the material familiar, but it doesn’t necessarily allow you to recall it when you need it. Active recall includes: closing the material and writing a three-sentence summary; speaking out the gist, details, responsibilities and next steps after listening; explaining a concept without looking at the notes; letting a chunk of words enter two new situations; reproducing the minimum running steps when there is no sample code; asking readers or peers to retell the meaning they really received. Recalling doesn’t have to be difficult to the point of failure every time. The ideal difficulty level is to allow the breach to occur while still being able to repair it. Too easy only creates a sense of flow, too difficult measures frustration, context or capacity. Recording "completions, prompts, times, errors, and responses" is more useful than recording "I worked hard today."

7. Feedback must enter the next action: more feedback is not better. Address 1-3 items first that will change the outcome of the task: Whether the audience understood, decided, or completed the intended action; Whether the facts, structure, or responsibilities were accurate; Which repeated errors are most worth fixing next time. Sentence-level feedback also distinguishes: necessary error correction, ambiguity, register selection, acceptable variations and style preferences. Let readers retell it first, and then discuss "whether it is natural". Feedbackers may identify blind spots and may have different backgrounds and goals; there must be reasons for adoption, partial adoption, rejection, and deferral. If the feedback only makes the old draft more beautiful, but does not change the actions in the new task, it cannot be counted as transfer. Write a piece of feedback as a condition for the next parallel task: change the topic, audience, voice, time, or constraints, and change only one variable.

8. Spacing, interleaving, and sleep: Retrieval practice and dispersed practice have more support in learning research, but there is no fixed calendar that works for everyone and all materials. You can use the current day, day 1, day 3-7, day 14 and day 30 as reminders, and then adjust according to performance: Easy and accurate, can also be used in new situations: extend the interval or increase the change; Effortful but successful: keep the interval similar; Repeated failures: reduce materials, shorten the interval or catch up on prior knowledge; only recognize it but not use it: increase output and cross-modal tasks; Continuous decline in body capacity: downshift, pause or ask for help, do not interpret recovery as laziness. You can stagger learning different skills, but don't change too many variables at the same time each time you practice, otherwise you won't know which layer is causing the change. Sleep, eating, exercise, and task-free time are not rewards after learning, but inputs for memory, attention, and recovery for the next time. Persistent insomnia, emotional or physical problems require qualified medical or psychological professional support, and this book does not make a diagnosis.
9. Keep the status outside the conversation: The chat, course, or app will end, and the learning status cannot just exist in it. Use the learning status template to stay:
Read the status first before taking actions in the next session; don't let the model guess the progress for you from old chats. Status files are fact pages, not diaries showing study efforts.

10. AI is a scaffold, not a result: AI can ask questions, explain, classify errors, generate counterexamples, simulate readers, provide parallel tasks and compare two versions. An auditable sequence is: Save your own tasks and first version first; Give the model only the minimum content required to complete the current diagnosis; Ask it to mark uncertainties, sources, and possible misjudgments; Return to primary materials, dictionaries, running results, teachers, peers, or real audiences for verification; Close the tool and complete it independently under new conditions; Write acceptance, rejection, and next steps back to the status file. Models cannot prove facts for you, assume privacy responsibilities, complete exams that prohibit outside help, or determine whether you have truly learned. Do not paste customer information, unpublished documents, certificates, medical privacy or unauthorized third-party content.

11. Make abilities move across conditions: Immediate performance only tells what happened under one condition. Transfer changes at least one thing: · Retention · Change · What to observe · · Task · Topic · Whether structure and strategies are still available · · Topic · Audience · Whether register, context and interpretation are adjusted · · Message · Modality · Whether listening, reading, speaking and writing support each other · · Genre · Time · Ability to retain threads and constraints under pressure · · Tools · Scaffolding · Can you continue independently after closing the prompt? · Only change one main condition at a time. If you replace them all, you won’t know whether the drop in results is due to difficulty, background, or method. Migration does not require that the new task be exactly the same as the old task, but that the core actions can still be called.

12. 7 days, 30 days, 12 weeks: 7 days: Make the first version happen Complete the first version of a real task; Do a complete learning loop three times; Classify a repeated error; Remove the most recent prompt on day 7 and do a similar task; Decide on only one condition to change next week. 30 days: Make the rhythm sustainable. Save a comparable output every week; alternate between old tasks and parallel tasks; delete activities that only create a sense of familiarity; repeatedly record sleep, capacity, time and real responses; retest under similar conditions on the 30th day, and write down any conclusions that cannot be drawn. 12 weeks: Bringing ability into life. Save similar samples in weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12; add unfamiliar topics, real audiences, or time pressure in the middle; complete meetings, exam simulations, document verification, email delivery, or work release at the end; use the results to decide to continue, downshift, change variables, or stop, instead of automatically upgrading the difficulty.

13. One-page general diagnosis: When completing a general diagnosis, follow the following order: Choose a real topic and four tasks; Record the conditions and complete the first version of listening, reading, speaking, and writing respectively; Write only one error that most affects the results for each item; Select an evidence card for each item and do a directed repair; Complete the parallel task on the 7th day, and repeat a real delivery on the 30th day; Write down which ability has changed, which one has not, and which one still has no evidence. Don’t simply average the four scores into one personality judgment. People who are reading B2 and speaking A2 do not need to find a "real level" first, but need to match the next task to the corresponding evidence.

Source and Boundary: Dunlosky et al. (2013), Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: A review of ten learning techniques, and discusses generalizability based on learning conditions, learners, materials and measurement tasks; it has a higher evaluation of practice tests and distributed exercises, and has better effects on activities such as repetition and highlighting. Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning: Comparing test versus repeated learning in a study of prose materials, reporting differences in delayed retention; samples, materials, and measurements cannot directly infer the same effects for all tasks. Cepeda et al. (2006), Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis of distributed practice in verbal recall tasks; optimal intervals depend on retention goals, materials, and tasks. Hattie & Timperley (2007), The Power of Feedback: Analyze differences in feedback type, timing, and delivery methods; "Feedback is effective" does not mean adding comments indiscriminately. Rasch & Born (2013), About Sleep's Role in Memory: A review of research on sleep and memory consolidation; individual needs, health conditions, and real-life routines still need to be judged separately. Pashler et al. (2008), Learning Styles: A review found insufficient evidence to support fixation on visual/…

Conclusion: Leave the method to next time: The most tempting thing about a learning style is that it looks like a shortcut. But any method can only truly belong to you when it can still help you complete the task after you close the information, leave the prompt, and change the topic. You don’t have to memorize the names of all the researchers, and you don’t have to turn your life into a constant survey. It's enough to remember a simple circuit: do it once independently and let difficulties arise; get specific feedback; do it again after a period of time; change the conditions and see if your ability follows. A good method will not make you better at explaining why you work hard, but will make you more capable of getting something done when no one reminds you. What remains in the end is not the name of the method, but that you still know how to start the next time you face an unfamiliar problem.

items.title: Vocabulary: From familiarity to calling in real tasks
items.core: Starting from the first encounter baseline, word search decision-making, meaning and collocation verification, use silent calling, misuse repair and delayed migration to build a truly usable vocabulary system.
body: Quick overview of this chapter: Define the real task first, do not use isolated vocabulary to replace situational ability; Save the first encounter baseline to distinguish between "not knowing the word" and "knowing but not parsing the sentence"; Make decisions about letting go, inferring, quick checking, learning or professional verification of unknown items; Learn word form, sound, current meaning, collocation, grammatical behavior, register and concept separately; Use unprompted recall, limited time recall and real audience result acceptance instead of the familiarity after reading the answer; Let the interval adjust with errors and usage results, and do not pretend that fixed dates are memory laws; use dictionaries, corpora, current documents, and field personnel to check AI-generated candidates; only track one topic, one first encounter sample, and one parallel task for fourteen days.

1. Define the task first, don’t pursue the total amount first: “Expanding vocabulary” cannot tell you what to learn today. First write clearly the conditions under which the language will work: · Task · Required vocabulary skills · Observable results · · Listening to meetings · Divide keyword chunks and responsibility relationships in natural speaking speed · Able to repeat decisions, risks, responsible persons and deadlines · · Read documents · Identify terms, actions and limitations in the current version · Able to complete minimal verification and point out the source location · · Oral explanation · Call appropriate chunks and fix them under time pressure · The audience can repeat the gist instead of guessing from the manuscript · · Write an email · Choose the precise meaning, collocation and relational tone · The recipient knows what to do and when to respond · · Take the test · Identify or produce a specified range by question type · Complete new questions, not just recognize old cards · The same person can understand the terms in a certain field, but cannot call them out in a meeting; the same person can also speak everyday words but cannot distinguish the synonyms in a contract. First determine the audience, materials, time constraints, allowed tools, and completion standards before knowing whether to test acceptance or output, breadth or precision. Use vocabulary evidence cards to put tasks, first encounters, verifications, calls, feedback, and delayed transfers on the same page.

2. Save an unmodified first encounter: Choose a material that is close to your real task: a 150-300 word essay, 60-90 seconds of audio, an email, an interface document, or a brief explanation. First record the allowed subtitles, dictionary, translation, search and AI, and then complete the first input or output without looking up words.

Don’t immediately attribute all failures to vocabulary. A sentence may fail because of unsegmented sounds, unclear syntactic scope, insufficient background knowledge, complex layout, or reduced concentration. Leave the original fill-in-the-blanks, retellings, recordings, or writing samples, and you will know later what the word search has changed. The first encounter with the baseline is not a shame list either. It simply answers: which meanings have already been reached before the tool intervenes, which places require guesswork, and which words actually block the task.

3. Make five decisions about unknowns: Not every new word is worthy of long-term review. When reading or hearing an unknown item, decide first: · Decision · Applicable conditions · Minimum record · · Let it go · Does not affect the gist, decision and safety, just a one-time detail · Why it can be skipped · · Contextual inference · Sufficient syntax, contrast, examples or context clues · Candidate meanings and confidence · · Quick review · Block current understanding, but low future use value · Current meaning and source · · Active learning · Recurring, mission-critical, will be used in the next two weeks · Sound, collocation, retrieval clues and retest · Professional verification · Involving safety, legal, medical, financial, version or business responsibilities · First-hand definition, scope of application and responsible person · Infer first and then verify, you can practice contextual judgment; but do not sacrifice safety and facts for the sake of "insisting on not searching words". Low risk readings can tolerate uncertainty, high risk operations must go back to current primary documentation or qualified personnel. Only 5-8 high-value word chunks are selected for active learning in one round. The selection is not based on how advanced it looks, but on the following: it appears repeatedly, blocks tasks, can be connected to existing languages, and can be used quickly.

4. A word contains at least eight questions: "English = Chinese" only records one candidate correspondence. More complete vocabulary knowledge includes: · Dimensions · Questions to ask · Examples or evidence · · Word form · How is it spelled, inflected and derived? · analyze → analysis → analytical · · Sound · How do stress, phonemes and conjunctions appear? · Listen and locate without subtitles · · Current meaning · What does it mean in this sentence? · Explain in your own words, do not list all meanings · · Collocations/Word Chunks · Which words does it usually complete the meaning with? · pose a risk to, meet a deadline · · Grammatical behavior · What structure follows, and who can be the subject? · Comparing the original sentence with a structure · · Register and pragmatics · Are formality, politeness, stance and identity appropriate? · kids / children / minors · · Concept and reference · Are the objects or systems referred to in reality really the same? · Version, domain definition or counterexample · · Calling condition · How long does it take to recall it? Do you need the initials or the original sentence? · Time-limited speaking and writing without prompts · Word families are estimation tools, not automatic mastering. help, helps, helped, helpful, helpless can be classified as a word family in some studies, but learners may not know the meaning, collocation and mood of each derived form. Abbreviations, interface names and fixed expressions in professional fields need to be checked against the current version. Words rarely work alone, either. Prioritize learning combinations that can bear the task: collocations, sentence blocks, word formation relationships, sentence pattern slots...

5. The meaning is not the first line in the list: polysemy is the easiest to create the illusion of "clearly understanding but mispronounced". When searching for words, keep the original sentence first and then compare:

Don’t mechanically transfer the Chinese definition on the first page of the dictionary into every situation. Learner's dictionary is suitable for looking at common meanings, pronunciation, grammatical marks, collocations and examples; real corpus can be used to check whether expressions appear in similar scenarios; technical terms should be returned to current official documents, standards or codes. Translation can help with comparison, but be wary of a native word covering multiple English concepts, or two institutional words that seem to correspond but have different scopes of application. In high-stakes texts, "roughly synonymous" is not an acceptable acceptance criterion.

6. Receptive vocabulary is not equal to productive vocabulary: receptive reading is understanding after seeing, receptive listening is segmenting and understanding sounds when they appear; productive speaking and writing require active calling when no answer is presented, and processing word forms, collocations and registers. Webb (2008) used corresponding receptive and productive translation tests to study second language learners and reported that the receptive vocabulary size was generally larger than the productive size, and the gap widened under the complete knowledge score in lower-frequency word segments. It shows that "knowing when you see it" cannot be directly translated into "using it when needed", but the specific gap is still affected by test format, scoring, learners and word frequency range. There are four steps to push a new word chunk from acceptance to production: explain the current meaning in the original sentence; close the original sentence and complete the blank filling or retelling according to situational clues; retain the function and change the character, time, theme or tone; call it in real emails, meetings, instructions, code reviews or conversations, and observe the other party's reaction. If the training sentence can only be reproduced, it is not considered transfer; if the meaning can be expressed but the combination is stiff, it means that the concept has been reached but the form still needs to be repaired. Locate the error in specific dimensions and don’t just write “I didn’t memorize it well”.

7. Correctly understand the coverage figures: The old version once wrote "1000 words are understood by 75%" and "7000 words are close to 90%". These unconditional equations, which mix counting units, corpora, modalities, and definitions of “comprehension,” are no longer retained in this edition. Vocabulary studies often discuss 95% and 98% running word coverage. As an intuition, 95% is approximately equal to 1 unknown item for every 20 words, and 98% is approximately 1 unknown item for every 50 words; however, whether the unknown items are concentrated in key positions, whether the background is familiar, and whether the syntax is complex will significantly change the actual difficulty. Schmitt, Jiang, and Grabe (2011) asked 661 participants from 8 countries to read two texts and complete vocabulary and comprehension measures. They found that the proportion of known words has a roughly linear relationship with comprehension, and there is no clear threshold for a sudden jump in understanding after a certain ratio; the authors believe that 98% is a more reasonable goal for academic texts. It is a group relationship, not an individual pass. Nation (2006) built a list of 1,000 word families based on the British National Corpus, and on the premise that "unaided comprehension requires 98% coverage", estimated that written texts require about 8000-9000 word families, and spoken texts require about 6000-7000 word families. Numbers depend on word family definitions, corpora, and premises, and cannot directly become a unified goal for all learners, fields, and tasks. Coverage is suitable to help select materials: if the unknown items are too dense and each one is critical, reduce the difficulty, shorten the text, or fill in the background; if most unknown items do not affect the main line, continue reading without turning each page into a vocabulary list.
8. High-quality vocabulary cards test only one decision: the front of the card should ask for recall, not re-reading of the answer:

The back should retain: pose a risk to the position of a reliable source; current meaning, pronunciation, part of speech, and register; a second scene of one's own; a confusing expression and difference; a reminder to remove on the next retest. Cards that are too long turn review back into reading. If a failure involves pronunciation, meaning and collocation, split it into different clues; if a card always depends on the original sentence to answer correctly, use a clue that is closer to the real task. The two-way translation card can be the starting point, but it should not be the end point. Authentic invocation requires moving from an intention, scene, or object toward an expression, rather than always starting from another linguistic label.

9. Let spacing follow performance: Forgetting is real, and there is no fixed "memory curve calendar" that works for all words and everyone. Checkpoints can be set on the same day, day 1, days 3-7, days 14 and 30, and then adjusted based on the evidence: Answer in seconds and can use it accurately in new sentences: extend the interval; Recall is laborious but correct: maintain or slightly extend; Meanings or synonyms are repeatedly confused: add comparisons and counterexamples; Cannot be heard but understood: add audio clues without text; Card answers are correct but cannot be used in real tasks: pause new additions and switch to time-limited speaking and writing; Continuous failure: remove cards, reduce the quantity, or make up concepts, sounds, and backgrounds; No longer relevant to the task: archive it and not review it permanently due to "sunk costs". Webb, Yanagisawa, and Uchihara's (2020) meta-analysis included 22 studies, 100 effect sizes, and examined intentional vocabulary activities such as flashcards, word lists, writing, and fill-in-the-blanks. The abstract reported average gains in immediate meaning/form recall of 60.1%/58.5%, which dropped to 39.4%/25.1% on the delayed test, with results varying widely across activities. It supports "deliberate practice can work and forgetfulness" and does not support any guarantee of decks, intervals, or individual results. Anki can perform interval scheduling, but the tool is not the method itself. Card count, punch streaks, and mature word count are only worth recording if they change the decision to "continue, split, migrate, or stop."

10. Use mistakes to determine the next round of exercises: Classify each low score first: · Error · Possible gap · Minimum repair for the next time · · Can’t see the word form · Spelling, derivation or inflection · Mark the root and part of speech and put it into a new sentence · · Unable to hear · Phoneme, stress, continuous reading or boundary · Compare the short audio, and then remove the text · · Misjudgment of meaning · Only remember the first meaning or ignore the context · Contrast and counterexamples of meaning items · · Stiff collocations · Only learn isolated words · Learn complete word chunks and check similar corpus · · Inconsistent register · Ignore relationships, formality or stance · Write two audience versions of the same intention · · Call too slow · The clues do not match the true intention · Set up 3-5 seconds of situational prompts and answer orally · · Transfer failure · Rely on the original sentence, theme or modality · Re-produce it by changing the subject, voice or task · Ask a real reader or listener to retell the received meaning first, and then discuss "whether it is natural". Vocabulary feedback should distinguish between necessary repairs that would change facts or relationships, acceptable variations, register choices, and personal style. Not every expression that is more native-like is better suited to the author and the situation.

11. AI can generate candidates, but cannot be responsible for words: AI is suitable for: generating fill-in-the-blanks based on situations, comparing synonymous expressions, simulating different audiences, providing counterexamples, classifying errors, and generating parallel tasks. The order of use: first save the first encounter and your own candidates; let AI explain which level of meaning each suggestion changes; require marking uncertainty, regional or register differences; return to dictionaries, real corpus, current documents or field personnel for verification; turn off AI and call it in new situations for a limited time; record adoption, rejection and reasons. Models may generate nonexistent collocations, incorrect etymologies, bogus quotes, or outdated technical definitions. Don’t give models customer data, unpublished documents, exam answers, or unauthorized third-party content. High risk terms are adjudicated by current primary sources and responsible persons.

12. The technical vocabulary is an index, not a course: the vocabulary in this warehouse is used to enter from tasks, not the number that must be completed every day. Goals: · Vocabulary · Task entry · · Common · Daily communication and cross-topic work · · Prompt · AI tasks, constraints and acceptance language · · Vibe Coding · Agent collaboration and code review · · JavaScript · Browser, front-end and asynchronous process · Python · Data, Automation and Scripting · · Go · Server, Concurrency and Deployment · · Java · JVM and Enterprise Systems · · PHP · Web Backend and Legacy System Maintenance · · Rust · Ownership, Performance and System Programming · · Swift · Apple Platform and Application Development · Select 5-8 word chunks from the current task and record the document version and source; complete a speaking and writing break from the list; retest in a parallel task a week later. Languages, frameworks, and products are updated, and the list is not a substitute for official documentation or current results.

13. A 35-minute training unit: 5 minutes: write down the real task, audience, materials and completion criteria; 7 minutes: complete the first encounter without word search or prompt output; 6 minutes: decide to let go, infer, consult, learn or verify the unknown items; 7 minutes: check the meaning, sound, collocation and register of 5-8 word chunks; 7 minutes: close the material and speak or write in the changed situation; 3 Minutes: Record a major error and a reminder for next takedown. Completion is more important than quantity. If capacity is insufficient for the day, keep only one first encounter, one high-value chunk, and one silent sentence; don't use up real language use time to maintain the card system.

14. Fourteen-day vocabulary experiment: · Days · Actions · Evidence left behind · · 1 · Choose real topics and tasks, complete the first encounter · Original understanding/output, conditions and blocking points · · 2 · Make five types of decisions for unknown items · Let go, infer, consult, learn, check list · · 3 · Check the eight dimensions of high-value word chunks · Sense, sound, collocation, register and source · · 4 · Create clues that test only one decision · Word cards and withdrawal conditions · · 5 · Complete the blanks, retelling or short-writing without prompts · Calling time and error types · · 6 · Change a modality in listening, reading, speaking and writing · Acceptance/production gap · · 7 · Use real materials or audience acceptance · Comprehension, response and repair · · 8 · Archive low-value items, keep 5-8 · Selection reasons and capacity changes · · 9 · Compare synonyms, counterexamples or common misuses · Meaning boundaries and reasons for rejection · · 10 · Changing the audience and register for the same topic · Relationship and tone migration · · 11 · Changing the topic for the same task · Migration of word chunk structure · · 12 · Let AI/companions propose candidates and then verify them · Source verification and adoption records · · 13 · Complete real output under time pressure · Email, recording, explanation or review results · · 14 · Close old cards and prompts to complete parallel tasks · Retain, split, archive or redirect the basis · Fourteen days is not a vocabulary crash period. It only answers: After leaving the original sentences, cards and instant prompts, can you recognize, select the correct word chunks and call them in time in the changed task?

15. How to judge that vocabulary is becoming an ability: be able to retain the main thread when encountering it for the first time and not be hijacked by each unknown word; be able to judge whether a word should be let go, inferred, quick-checked, studied, or professionally verified; be able to explain the current meaning, origin, collocation, register, and counterexamples instead of just memorizing the translation; be able to segment in natural sounds and recognize word forms in text; be able to call it in a limited time after closing the answer; the meaning, relationship, and next step received by the real reader or listener are consistent with the intention; Errors can be located and moved to the next exercise instead of just increasing the number of cards; it can still be transferred after changing the topic, audience, mode or task; words that are no longer important can be archived and focus can be returned to the current life. Vocabulary growth doesn't always mean lists get longer. Sometimes it takes the form of knowing which word to let go first when reading, knowing which word to say accurately in a meeting, or knowing when writing an email that a more flowery expression wouldn't fit the current relationship. You are no longer stuck with all the unknowns at once, nor are you masking failed calls with familiarity.

Sources and Boundaries: Nation (2006), How Large a Vocabulary Is Needed for Reading and Listening?: Estimated size required for unaided comprehension based on word family list from the British National Corpus with 98% coverage assumption; extrapolation of counting units, corpus, proper name treatment and comprehension criteria limits. Schmitt, Jiang & Grabe (2011), The Percentage of Words Known in a Text and Reading Comprehension: A 661-person, 8-country sample shows a roughly linear relationship between coverage and reading comprehension, with no clear mutation threshold found; it does not constitute a guarantee for individuals or other genres. Webb (2008), Receptive and Productive Vocabulary Sizes of L2 Learners: Comparing receptive and productive knowledge with corresponding translation tests; results are limited by test direction, scoring, word frequency, and sample conditions. Webb, Yanagisawa & Uchihara (2020), How Effective Are Intentional Vocabulary-Learning Activities?: Meta-analysis pooled 22 studies, 100 effect sizes, showing clear differences between immediate and delayed recall and across activities; average results are not guaranteed for fixed intervals or individual learning. Pashler et al. (2008), Learning Styl…

Conclusion: Let the word arrive when needed: What really remains in the memory is often not the first line of the dictionary definition, but the moment when you needed it: explaining a risk to a companion, asking for help from a stranger, apologizing to someone close to you, or finally understanding a page of text that you could only avoid in the past. A vocabulary can preserve order for you, but it cannot live for you. Only when a word enters sounds, sentences, relationships and consequences can it change from collection to ability. It doesn’t have to stay forever; some words can be filed away after a period of work, and some words will slowly grow into your own tone as you use them over and over again. There is no rush to own the entire language. Let a few words you really need come to you first, even when there are no answers. They are not responsible for proving that you are smart, they are only responsible for helping you take another step closer to the world where the meaning is about to be interrupted.

items.title: Grammar: Let structure serve meaning
items.core: Starting from real tasks and unmodified samples, the grammar is reduced to the selection of time, participants, certainty, cause and effect, and information focus, and use comparison, output, feedback, delayed retesting, and transfer to establish usable structures.
body: Quick overview of this chapter: Grammar is first and foremost about the selection of meanings and relationships, not a collection of terms; Save the first version of the real task before deciding which rule to learn; Distinguish between changing meaning, blocking tasks, recurrences, register incompatibility and low-impact errors; Explicit explanations can help see the structure clearly, but must be re-entered into meaningful output; Build a transferable foundation with minimal sentence skeleton, time and aspect, noun reference, modality, clause connection and information focus; AI You can compare versions, generate parallel exercises and classify errors, but important judgments still need to be reviewed by dictionaries, corpora, teachers or real readers; only one structural issue is tracked in fourteen days, and there is no need to complete the entire grammar at once.
1. Grammar is not about making sentences more complicated: the following three sentences are very short, but bear different relationships:

The difference is not in "which sentence is more advanced". They answer respectively: what happened in the past; whether the current result has been established; what conditions future actions depend on. Look Again:

Structure changes responsibility, focus, and narrative perspective. Grammatical choices affect how readers interpret events and whether the author hides his or her actions outside of the sentence. Therefore, when learning grammar, first ask: What does this structure help the audience know more, or what misunderstandings are avoided? If you can only recite the name but cannot explain its meaning in the task, learning has not yet entered into use.

2. Start with six categories of meaning selection: There is no need to advance evenly according to the traditional grammar book catalog. In true expression, the following six types of choices are more likely to expose current gaps: · Questions of meaning · Common structures · Task questions that need to be answered · · Who participates, who is responsible · Subject, object, active/passive, pronoun · Who did the action? Who is affected? Are responsibilities hidden? · · Time and status · Tense, progressive, perfect, time adverbials · When did things happen? Does it last? Do the current results hold? · · What object · Article, singular and plural, countability, determiner · Is it the first mention, a specific object, a general category, or a quantity? · · Negation and questions · Auxiliary verbs, interrogative words, scope of negation · Is it negating action, degree or condition? What part is the question really asking about? · · Relationships and logic · Parallelism, clauses, conditions, cause and effect, concession · Which thing is a cause, condition, background, contrast or result? · · Certainty and attitude · Modal verbs, adverbs, moderating expressions · Is this a fact, a possibility, a suggestion, an obligation, a hypothesis or a polite request? · A mission usually exposes only one or two of these categories. Work on the choices that change the outcome of the task first, instead of starting over from the entire grammar book just because you see an error.

3. Save a baseline with a real task: Choose a task that you will actually do in the near future: write an email, explain a project, tell an experience, retell an article, make a request, answer an interview question, or attend a meeting. Complete the first version within a time limit without checking the grammar answers or letting AI rewrite it. You can use one of three samples: Speaking: speak unscripted for 90–120 seconds and transcribe; Writing: write 150–250 words in 15–20 minutes; Comprehension: read or listen to a short passage of authentic material, highlight any structural relationships you cannot explain, and reconstruct in your own words. Then fill in:
